Record date: 2129-07-17
South Elizabeth Seychelles Hospital INTERNAL MEDICINE DEPARTMENT Location: 4923 Olivia Parkway Suite 217, Lake Jennabury
PATIENT: Lysander Fairfax Phone: 28451903 email:bradleymorgan@example.org DATE OF BIRTH: 1947-05-12 AGE: 80 years
FOLLOW-UP DATE: 07/17/29 FOLLOWED BY: Dr. Emily Carter
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Persistent shortness of breath, increased cough with yellowish sputum, and worsening bilateral lower extremity edema.
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Lysander Fairfax returns for follow-up after a week of adjustments to his treatment plan for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and congestive heart failure. He reports slight improvement in his respiratory symptoms, stating that the continuous nebulized albuterol has provided some relief; however, he continues to experience significant shortness of breath, particularly during exertion. The patient notes that he has been using his albuterol inhaler less frequently, now averaging 10 times per day, which is an improvement from previous usage.
Despite these changes, he has developed a persistent cough with yellowish sputum, which raises concern for potential secondary infection. He denies any further hemoptysis. The bilateral lower extremity edema remains problematic, with discomfort and pain exacerbated by prolonged standing. He reports that the increased furosemide regimen has led to some diuresis, but the edema has not resolved significantly. His insomnia persists, though he has been practicing cognitive-behavioral techniques as discussed during the last visit.
REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General - + fatigue, - weight gain, no fevers or chills. Pulmonary - + persistent shortness of breath, + increased productive cough with yellowish sputum, - hemoptysis. Cardiac - no chest pain or palpitations, + orthopnea, - paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Gastrointestinal - no nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Musculoskeletal - + joint pain, + persistent bilateral lower extremity edema. Neurological - no dizziness or headaches.
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: - Blood Pressure: 145/85 mmHg - Heart Rate: 88 bpm - Respiratory Rate: 22 breaths/min - Oxygen Saturation: 89% on room air
General: The patient appears in mild respiratory distress but is more comfortable than at the last visit.
HEENT: No nasal flaring, oropharynx clear.
Lungs: Diminished breath sounds bilaterally with wheezing; crackles are still present in the lower lung fields.
Cardiac: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs or gallops.
Extremities: Persistent bilateral lower extremity edema, with pitting noted, particularly in the calves.
ASSESSMENT
1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with partial response to treatment; concern for possible bacterial infection given the change in sputum color. 2. Congestive heart failure with moderate fluid overload; some improvement noted with increased furosemide. 3. Insomnia, with ongoing cognitive-behavioral strategies in place.
PLAN
1. Initiate a course of oral antibiotics with amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for 7 days to address the patient's productive cough and yellowish sputum, indicative of possible bacterial infection. 2. Continue nebulized albuterol every 2 hours and nebulized budesonide every 6 hours to manage airway inflammation. 3. Maintain furosemide at 120 mg daily; consider increasing to 160 mg if significant edema persists and diuresis is inadequate. 4. Monitor electrolyte levels, particularly potassium, due to the addition of spironolactone, which will now be prescribed at 25 mg daily to further assist with fluid retention. 5. Schedule a follow-up echocardiogram to evaluate cardiac function and monitor for any changes in the patient's heart failure status. 6. Continue to support cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia and assess the need for pharmacological intervention if symptoms do not improve. 7. Educate the patient on recognizing signs of worsening infection or heart failure, including increased shortness of breath, chest pain, or significant weight gain.
The patient demonstrated understanding of the revised treatment plan and expressed a commitment to adhering to the new medication regimen.
DISPOSITION
Mr. Fairfax was stable for discharge, with a follow-up appointment scheduled for 07/24/29. He was instructed to contact the office or seek immediate care should he experience any acute changes in his condition or new concerning symptoms.
